title: Should this process be automated?
summary: Start with the process and its error economics. Decide what evidence would justify automation, a bounded experiment, or keeping the work manual.

applicability.required: You are deciding whether to automate a process or expand an existing automation.
applicability.optional: Use a short evidence review for a small reversible experiment; deepen it as consequences and uncertainty grow.
applicability.unnecessary: Do not implement every pattern here. Omit mechanisms that do not address an identified requirement, and record the rationale.

prerequisites: A process owner and representative examples
A current baseline for time, errors and review

sections.title: Process mapping, users, stakeholders, goals, process owner, current pain and baseline
body: Observe a real case from request to resolution. Record who initiates it, who owns the outcome, each system touched, waiting time and rework. Ask users which step is painful before accepting a sponsor's solution. A useful baseline includes elapsed time and incorrect outcomes, not only time spent typing.

sections.title: Process simplification before automation; stable rules versus judgment and ambiguity
body: Remove redundant approvals and duplicate data entry before introducing a model. Write a decision table for stable rules; if the table handles the meaningful cases, conventional code is easier to test. Reserve probabilistic interpretation for ambiguity that cannot be resolved by improving the process or input form.

sections.title: Volume, variability, exceptions, seasonality, data readiness and access feasibility
body: Sample ordinary and exceptional cases across busy and quiet periods. Check whether required data can actually be accessed under the intended identity, with reliable identifiers and sufficient freshness. A demonstration on ten clean documents tells little about scanned tables, missing fields, spikes or permissions in the live process.

sections.title: Manual versus conventional automation versus fixed AI workflow versus autonomous agent
body: Compare four credible baselines on the same cases: manual handling, ordinary rules, a fixed sequence containing model calls, and a tool-using agent. Add autonomy only when variable next steps create measurable value. A classification call inside an existing service does not require an agent runtime.

sections.title: Error economics: wrong action, missed action, delay, escalation, review and rework
body: Separate the costs of acting incorrectly, failing to act, responding late, escalating and repairing damage. Estimate frequency and consequence separately; a rare irreversible error can dominate many small time savings. Include the human time needed to inspect plausible but incorrect output, which can exceed the time to do the task.

sections.title: Success criteria, acceptance thresholds, scope, exclusions, autonomy levels
body: Write observable acceptance thresholds with the process owner: which outcomes count, which inputs are excluded, and what the system may do without approval. Distinguish reading information, preparing drafts, executing an approved action and choosing actions autonomously. Define what happens when the acceptance evidence is missing.

sections.title: Reversibility, impact, human capacity, opportunity cost, feasibility, ROI
body: Ask whether an action can be undone in business terms, not just technically. An email can be deleted from a sent folder but cannot be unread. Estimate review demand at peak volume and compare it with staffed capacity. Include integration, maintenance, opportunity cost and residual risk in feasibility.

sections.title: Prioritization, small experiments, stop/continue criteria, validating real adoption
body: Run a small experiment with a fixed time and spend limit, representative cases, and a decision date. Specify stop conditions before seeing results. Measure whether users actually adopt the output and whether total turnaround improves. A successful demo is evidence for the next experiment, not permission for unrestricted release.

sections.title: How to say "we need more evidence" or "do not automate this."
body: Use an evidence request with an owner and deadline: 'We cannot assess automatic approval until we measure exception rates and define who handles disputes.' Recommend no automation when the process lacks ownership, required data is inaccessible, or consequences cannot be contained. Preserve a manual path while uncertainty is investigated.

alternatives.name: Manual handling
alternatives.benefits: Retains expert judgment for rare ambiguous work

alternatives.name: Autonomous agent
alternatives.limitations: Only justified by measured task value

tradeoffs: Manual handling: retains expert judgment for rare ambiguous work; costs include labor and queue time. Does not scale without staffing.
Conventional rules: predictable and straightforward to test; costs include rule maintenance. Brittle when exceptions dominate.
Fixed AI workflow: adds interpretation inside explicit steps; costs include evaluation and review. Still needs deterministic boundaries.
Autonomous agent: adapts next steps to evidence; costs include higher operational complexity. Only justified by measured task value.
decisionCriteria: Can simpler rules solve the meaningful cases?

examples.title: Hypothetical worked example
examples.body: A hypothetical invoice intake team spends four minutes copying fields and twenty minutes resolving missing purchase orders. A model that saves copying time may barely change turnaround. First improve purchase-order matching and define who resolves exceptions; then compare extraction against a manual baseline.

failureModes.symptom: The demo works but nobody adopts it
failureModes.cause: The experiment optimized a visible step rather than the real bottleneck
failureModes.diagnostic: Compare end-to-end turnaround and reviewer effort with the original baseline
failureModes.mitigation: Pause expansion and observe real cases with the process owner

verification: Record evidence for: Who owns the outcome?
Record evidence for: Can simpler rules solve the meaningful cases?
Record evidence for: Are error consequences reversible?
Record evidence for: Can humans handle peak escalations?
Exercise the failure case: the demo works but nobody adopts it. Preserve the observed outcome and unresolved limitations.
reconsiderWhen: Task volume, exception mix or consequence changes

title: Design boundaries around probabilistic decisions
summary: Keep business rules, state and authority explicit while models handle the uncertain parts of a workflow.

applicability.required: A model's output influences business state, crosses system boundaries or must be maintained by a team.
applicability.optional: Use a short evidence review for a small reversible experiment; deepen it as consequences and uncertainty grow.
applicability.unnecessary: Do not implement every pattern here. Omit mechanisms that do not address an identified requirement, and record the rationale.

sections.title: SOLID, separation of concerns, explicit contracts, domain boundaries, dependency inversion
body: Keep business policy separate from model adapters, prompts, storage and transport. Domain code should depend on small interfaces that express business operations. Apply SOLID where it improves change isolation; do not create a class hierarchy for every prompt. A mock model should let you test policy without network calls.

sections.title: Typed inputs/outputs plus semantic validation; schema validity is not correctness
body: A valid JSON object can still contain the wrong customer, amount or date. First validate structure and types, then check semantic constraints against authoritative data. Reject identifiers the caller cannot access, impossible values and inconsistent field combinations before any side effect. Return actionable validation errors without leaking other tenants' data.

sections.title: Business invariants, explicit state/transitions, authoritative systems, ownership
body: Represent meaningful states explicitly: proposed, awaiting approval, executing, outcome unknown, verified, failed or cancelled. Define permitted transitions and the component authorized to make each transition. The business system owns the transaction outcome; a model's completion message is not an authoritative state update.

sections.title: Deterministic rules around probabilistic decisions; bounded autonomy
body: Use models to propose interpretations or plans while deterministic code enforces authorization, budgets and invariants. Bound allowed tools, objects and action sizes. Escalate ambiguous cases to a person. This boundary remains necessary even when model quality improves, because fluent output does not prove intent or permission.

sections.title: Synchronous/API, queued, scheduled, event-driven, and long-running execution
body: Choose an API response for work that fits the caller's deadline; return a job identifier for longer work. Queues absorb variation but create operational duties. Schedules suit periodic batches; events suit changes from other systems. Long approvals need persisted state rather than an open HTTP connection.

sections.title: Distributed-system fundamentals: consistency, concurrency, transaction boundaries
body: Identify the transaction boundary before distributing work. A database commit and an external API call usually cannot be made atomic together. Plan for stale reads, simultaneous changes and partial failure. Use version checks or locks for invariants, and reconcile external outcomes rather than assuming a network response settles everything.

sections.title: Build only necessary abstraction; one step does not imply one agent
body: Begin with one deployable service and explicit functions when that meets the need. Split a component when it needs a distinct scaling, security or ownership boundary. One processing step can be a function, not an agent. Keep abstractions tied to a demonstrated second use or concrete substitution requirement.

sections.title: Deployment boundaries, modularity, portability, maintainability, change isolation
body: Put provider-specific request shapes behind adapters and keep persisted state in documented application formats. Test migration and export before lock-in becomes expensive. Separate deployment boundaries only where independent release or isolation pays for the extra operational burden. Document failure behavior at each boundary.

sections.title: Risk-proportionate design, uncertainty, architectural decision records
body: Record a short architecture decision: context, alternatives, chosen trade-off, assumptions, evidence and revisit trigger. Match design effort to consequence and uncertainty. A reversible internal draft helper can tolerate a simpler operating model than an action-taking workflow that changes many customers' records.

alternatives.name: Single service
alternatives.limitations: May need separation as boundaries change

tradeoffs: Single service: simple ownership and debugging; costs include shared scaling unit. May need separation as boundaries change.
Queued worker: handles longer tasks and bursts; costs include queue and recovery operations. Acceptance is not completion.
Durable workflow: explicit state across interruptions; costs include replay and versioning constraints. External effects still need reconciliation.
decisionCriteria: How does a caller learn the final outcome?
Which changes must be independently deployable?

examples.title: Hypothetical worked example
examples.body: In a hypothetical .NET service, a model returns a suggested account classification through an adapter. Domain code checks the account exists, the caller owns it and the transition is allowed. A queue worker commits the approved update with an operation ID, independent of the wording of the model's answer.

examples.title: A concrete state contract
examples.body: Hypothetical notification state table: proposed -> awaiting approval only after target validation; awaiting approval -> ready only with an unexpired approval matching the action hash; ready -> dispatched after reserving an operation ID; dispatched -> verified only after provider status confirms the intended recipient; dispatched -> outcome unknown on timeout. Outcome unknown may move to verified, confirmed-not-sent or manual reconciliation. Cancellation stops new dispatch but does not erase an in-flight send. Record transitions with actor, timestamp and expected state version.

failureModes.symptom: Valid JSON produces an invalid business action
failureModes.cause: Structural validation was mistaken for domain correctness
failureModes.diagnostic: Inspect the entity, caller ownership, expected version and invariant checks
failureModes.mitigation: Reject the action and enforce semantic checks at the domain boundary

verification: Record evidence for: Which component owns each invariant?
Record evidence for: Where can partial failure occur?
Record evidence for: How does a caller learn the final outcome?
Record evidence for: Which changes must be independently deployable?
Exercise the failure case: valid json produces an invalid business action. Preserve the observed outcome and unresolved limitations.
reconsiderWhen: New side effects, scale or deployment boundaries

title: Choose a workflow and delegation pattern
summary: Match coordination to dependencies. Make ownership, stopping and result verification explicit before adding agents.

applicability.required: The task has multiple dependent steps, workers, handoffs or a variable execution path.
applicability.optional: Use a short evidence review for a small reversible experiment; deepen it as consequences and uncertainty grow.
applicability.unnecessary: Multi-agent coordination is unnecessary when one function, workflow or restricted agent meets the acceptance criteria.

prerequisites: A shared budget and result contract

sections.title: Sequential pipelines/prompt chaining, routing, fan-out/fan-in, aggregation
body: Use a sequence when each result is an input to the next step; validate between steps to avoid amplifying errors. Route to specialized processing when categories are distinguishable. Fan out independent subtasks and define how fan-in handles missing or late results. Aggregation must preserve disagreements that matter.

sections.title: Orchestrator–workers, handoffs, plan/execute, evaluator–optimizer
body: An orchestrator can discover subtasks dynamically, but each worker still needs a bounded contract. A handoff changes responsibility; a plan/execute split separates proposing steps from carrying them out. An evaluator–optimizer loop is useful only with an actionable rubric, a maximum effort and a stopping condition.

sections.title: Human interrupt/resume, durable state machines, saga/compensating actions
body: Persist an approval request and release the worker while a person decides. On resume, reload current business state before executing. Model multistep business operations as states with explicit recovery; compensating actions are new business actions with their own failure modes, not a magical transaction rollback.

sections.title: Single-agent/multitool versus multi-agent; dependencies and parallelizability
body: Try one agent with a restricted tool set before distributing responsibility. Separate agents when tasks are independently checkable, contexts differ substantially, or policy boundaries require isolation. Parallel execution helps only where inputs are available and shared writes do not create races. Measure total work as well as elapsed time.

sections.title: Task boundaries, ownership, delegation contracts, outputs, tools and context
body: Give every delegated task an objective, permitted inputs and tools, output schema, evidence requirement, deadline and owner. State what is out of scope. Return artifact references with version or hash when outputs are large. The parent verifies the result against its contract before including it in the final answer.

sections.title: Conflicting results, correlated model errors, shared-state races
body: Two agents agreeing can share the same mistaken source or model bias. Compare evidence and resolve conflicts explicitly; voting is not an independent truth test. For shared writes, partition ownership or use concurrency controls. Never let the final synthesizer silently overwrite a material unresolved disagreement.

sections.title: Parent/child lifecycle, shared resource budgets, depth/width limits
body: Allocate the entire task a common time, call and cost budget, then reserve portions for children. Enforce maximum concurrent children and delegation depth in code. Track each child's parent, status and resources. Parent failure must not leave orphaned workers acting indefinitely.

sections.title: Repeated handoff, stalled convergence, cancellation propagation, stopping
body: Detect repeated tasks and handoffs with stable task IDs and an explicit progress measure. Stop or escalate when attempts consume budget without producing new evidence. Cancellation must reach queued and running descendants. A child's 'blocked' result should name the missing input so the parent can change the plan.

sections.title: Asynchronous versus synchronous coordination trade-offs
body: Synchronous coordination is easier to follow but waits for slow workers. Asynchronous messages improve responsiveness while introducing ordering, stale results and cancellation races. Choose based on dependency structure and operational capacity. Tag results with the task version so an old answer cannot satisfy a revised request.

sections.title: Pattern examples and failure modes; avoid multi-agent complexity without evidence
body: In a hypothetical document comparison, independent workers inspect separate documents and return quoted evidence locations; a deterministic merger flags conflicts. In a shared editing task, concurrent workers can corrupt assumptions about the same file. Anthropic's research case reported overdelegation and duplicated work; treat that as a scoped lesson, not a universal performance ratio.

tradeoffs: Sequential pipeline: clear dependencies and checkpoints; costs include serial latency. Bad early outputs can cascade.
Fan-out / fan-in: concurrent independent work; costs include aggregation and partial failures. Shared writes need coordination.
Orchestrator–workers: discovers subtasks dynamically; costs include delegation overhead. Needs bounded ownership and budgets.
Evaluator–optimizer: targeted refinement; costs include more calls and judge errors. Requires measurable stopping criteria.
decisionCriteria: What happens when a child is late?

examples.title: Hypothetical worked example
examples.body: A hypothetical release review has independent security and operations evidence gathering, followed by one release decision. Gather those inputs in parallel, but do not parallelize two agents changing the same deployment configuration. Preserve unresolved disagreement for the release owner.

examples.title: Choose a pattern for each dependency
examples.body: Hypothetical report pipeline: parse -> extract -> validate is sequential because each step consumes the previous output. Inspect three independent source documents in fan-out workers, then fan-in with an explicit missing-result policy. Route known document types by validated metadata. Use an orchestrator only if the needed subtasks are not known until evidence arrives. An evaluator may request one correction with a concrete failed criterion; after the effort budget, preserve the unresolved issue rather than looping. A person approves the final recipient list before delivery.

failureModes.symptom: Agent stalls, repeats or delegates endlessly
failureModes.cause: Tasks lack ownership, measurable progress or a shared stopping budget
failureModes.diagnostic: Inspect repeated task IDs, unchanged artifacts and parent/child resource use
failureModes.mitigation: Cancel further delegation, preserve partial evidence and re-scope one bounded task

verification: Record evidence for: Are subtasks truly independent?
Record evidence for: What happens when a child is late?
Record evidence for: How are conflicting results handled?
Record evidence for: What stops the loop?
Exercise the failure case: agent stalls, repeats or delegates endlessly. Preserve the observed outcome and unresolved limitations.
reconsiderWhen: Repeated handoffs, conflicts or rising coordination cost

title: Select a framework without guessing
summary: Choose a layer first, enforce mandatory requirements, then compare representative proofs of concept.

applicability.required: You are adopting or replacing a runtime, integration platform, model or provider.
applicability.optional: Use a short evidence review for a small reversible experiment; deepen it as consequences and uncertainty grow.
applicability.unnecessary: Do not implement every pattern here. Omit mechanisms that do not address an identified requirement, and record the rationale.

prerequisites: A common proof-of-concept task and failure tests

sections.title: Discover current ecosystem rather than restrict to names from this discussion
body: Start with required behavior and search maintained official documentation, repositories and release notes across layers. Record the date and the exact product identity. Marketing names can describe an SDK, hosted service or unrelated tool. The comparison catalogue is a research snapshot; repeat checks before committing a production architecture.

sections.title: Compare conventional workflow engines, event platforms, agent runtimes, managed cloud platforms, low-code tools, and thin custom implementations
body: Conventional workflow engines primarily manage state and recovery; event platforms move events; agent runtimes manage model/tool loops. Managed platforms supply operations with provider constraints, low-code tools favor visual integration, and thin custom implementations favor direct control. These layers may be composed instead of treated as substitutes.

sections.title: Candidates to investigate, not predetermined winners: LangGraph/LangChain, Microsoft Agent Framework, CrewAI, Google ADK, PydanticAI, AutoGen where current, Semantic Kernel where current, LlamaIndex, Haystack, Agno, Strands, provider SDKs, Temporal, Azure Durable Functions, Dapr Workflow, n8n, and other relevant maintained options
body: The catalogue investigates the named libraries as candidates rather than winners. Reduce the shortlist using language, deployment and mandatory behavior, then implement the same small task in two or three plausible options. Check persistence, approval resumption and side-effect recovery in runnable experiments rather than counting advertised features.

sections.title: Hindsight, Flue, Paperclip and similar products may occupy complementary layers; verify exact current scope and maturity
body: Memory products such as Hindsight, orchestration products such as Flue and organizational control products such as Paperclip may solve different problems. Verify the exact repository and scope first. A memory service does not automatically replace a durable workflow engine, and a management interface does not establish execution guarantees.

sections.title: Treat names as research leads; verify current status, successor/deprecation, version, license, features and production limitations
body: Capture a tested package version, license file, release activity and documented limitations for each shortlisted dependency. A documentation review is not a production qualification. Record successor or migration notices explicitly; do not infer support from a familiar name. Unchecked capabilities remain unverified and require an owner.

sections.title: Distinguish model, provider/router, SDK, harness, orchestrator, memory layer, retrieval system, and developer coding subscription
body: A model generates outputs; a provider serves models; a router chooses providers; an SDK wraps APIs; a harness runs a loop; an orchestrator coordinates work; retrieval locates evidence; memory persists selected information. A developer subscription is a purchasing arrangement, not necessarily authorization or capacity for a production API.

sections.title: Hard requirements: persistence, approvals, failure semantics, security, deployment, stack fit, operations, budget
body: Write pass/fail requirements before weighted preferences: supported deployment, identity controls, durable resumption, exact-action approval, recovery semantics, operational visibility and hard limits. A high convenience score cannot compensate for a failed mandatory requirement. Unknown evidence should block qualification until verified, not be scored as a proven failure.

sections.title: Team skills, maintainability, build/buy, managed/self-hosted, licensing, costs, lock-in, export and migration
body: Include the team's existing language and on-call skills, licensing obligations, managed service commitments, data export and exit cost. Buying reduces some maintenance but does not outsource business accountability. Self-hosting adds patching, recovery and capacity duties. Test moving one representative state artifact out of the chosen platform.

sections.title: Comparable POCs using common tasks, failure tests, budgets, and documented weights
body: Run comparable proofs of concept with identical task data, tool contracts, budgets and graders. Include a killed worker, delayed response, duplicated event and expired approval. Publish raw outcomes and weights. Repeat variable model cases; small score differences without uncertainty estimates should not decide an expensive migration.

sections.title: Model task quality, tool calling, structured outputs, latency, language/document needs, context and privacy
body: Evaluate models on your task's required languages, document formats, tool argument correctness, structured output and escalation behavior. Measure tail latency and cost per verified outcome. A larger context limit is not evidence of better use of all content. Public benchmarks are screening clues, not task acceptance tests.

sections.title: Routing, fallback equivalence, provider outages, model retirement, version pinning where possible
body: Test fallback on the same safety and output requirements as the primary model. A provider outage may change capability, data handling or latency when routed elsewhere. Define when to stop instead of falling back. Pin versions where supported, track retirement announcements and keep a regression suite ready for replacement.

sections.title: Prompting versus retrieval versus fine-tuning; choose the intervention matching the failure
body: Improve instructions when the task is unclear, retrieval when evidence is missing or stale, and consider fine-tuning when stable behavior needs many consistent examples. None fixes an unauthorized tool or incorrect source data. Diagnose the failure before purchasing a more elaborate intervention.

sections.title: Record assumptions and revisit criteria; never rank models solely on public benchmarks
body: Write why the selected option fits today, which capabilities were actually exercised, and what would reverse the decision. Revisit when task mix, provider terms, operating costs, team capacity or support status changes. Prefer explicit uncertainty to a permanent league table that hides different use cases.

alternatives.name: Agent runtime
alternatives.limitations: May not supply durable business effects

tradeoffs: Thin custom implementation: direct behavior and few abstractions; costs include you own runtime features. Can grow into accidental framework.
Agent runtime: reusable model and tool execution; costs include framework conventions. May not supply durable business effects.
Workflow engine: state and recovery semantics; costs include operational and replay model. Does not establish model quality.
Managed platform: reduces some hosting work; costs include provider terms and lock-in. Check export and deployment constraints.

examples.title: Hypothetical worked example
examples.body: For a hypothetical approval workflow that must survive a two-day wait, compare a durable engine with an agent runtime plus persistence. Kill the worker after a simulated write, restart it and inspect the business state. A polished chat demo does not answer this requirement.

examples.title: Hard gates before preferences
examples.body: Hypothetical selection sheet: durable resume after worker loss=required; approvals bound to exact parameters=required; chosen deployment/language=required; tenant isolation=required; exportable state=required. For each option record pass, fail or unverified with a dated artifact. One failed requirement excludes the option for this scope; one unverified requirement prevents qualification. Only then compare preferences such as team familiarity, implementation effort and operating cost with explicit weights. Repeat the same failure scenario in every candidate. Model/provider sheet: task quality, required tool/schema behavior, data handling, latency, quotas and fallback equivalence each need separate evidence.

failureModes.symptom: A chosen framework cannot resume an approval safely
failureModes.cause: Selection relied on feature names instead of failure tests
failureModes.diagnostic: Run the same suspended and killed-worker scenario against the shortlisted options
failureModes.mitigation: Keep actions manual until state and recovery semantics are verified

verification: Record evidence for: Which layer is actually missing?
Record evidence for: Which requirements are mandatory?
Record evidence for: Which claims have executable evidence?
Record evidence for: What is the exit plan?
Exercise the failure case: a chosen framework cannot resume an approval safely. Preserve the observed outcome and unresolved limitations.
reconsiderWhen: Support, license, provider behavior or team capacity changes

title: Keep the right context through long tasks
summary: Distinguish missing storage, missing retrieval and ignored evidence. Preserve goals and pending actions across compaction.

applicability.required: A task uses long histories, retrieved evidence, multiple tools or compaction.
applicability.optional: Use a short evidence review for a small reversible experiment; deepen it as consequences and uncertainty grow.
applicability.unnecessary: Do not implement every pattern here. Omit mechanisms that do not address an identified requirement, and record the rationale.

prerequisites: An input budget and representative long traces

sections.title: Clear instructions, examples, instruction hierarchy, structured outputs and grounding
body: Write the task, allowed scope, output contract and abstention behavior in clear language. Include a few varied examples with expected reasoning evidence, including an example that should escalate. Treat system instructions, user requests and retrieved documents as different trust levels; labeling untrusted text helps but cannot itself enforce policy.

sections.title: Context assembly: task, instructions, tools, history, state, retrieved evidence
body: Assemble context deliberately for each call: the active goal, constraints, permitted tools, relevant history, current execution state and supporting evidence. Keep authoritative values outside free-form conversation and refresh them when needed. Log which evidence identifiers were included so a wrong answer can be traced to its inputs.

sections.title: Token allocation, output/tool-result headroom, just-in-time retrieval
body: Budget for instructions, tool schemas, task data, history and retrieved excerpts, then reserve room for tool results and the final output. A maximum input budget should leave headroom for the next step. Measure real token use and truncation; a byte count or estimated word count is not exact token accounting.

sections.title: Sliding window, summarization, compaction, tool-result clearing, external artifacts
body: A sliding window is simple but can remove old constraints. Summaries reduce volume but may distort facts. Clearing bulky tool results works if stable artifacts retain necessary evidence. External references save context at the cost of retrieval latency. Choose by what the next step needs, not by maximizing filled context.

sections.title: Test preservation of goals, constraints, pending actions and evidence after compaction
body: Test compaction with cases whose critical constraint appears early and whose pending action is easy to repeat. After compaction, ask for the current goal, authorization, unresolved evidence, completed work and next action. Compare with the pre-compaction record. Preserve exact IDs and external side-effect status in structured state.

sections.title: Context isolation between projects, tenants, agents and trust levels
body: Partition context by tenant, project, task and trust boundary. Child agents receive only the inputs they need; shared caches must include authorization scope in their keys. A prompt saying 'do not reveal other users' is not isolation. Test requests with similar document titles across different tenants.

sections.title: Distinguish storage loss, retrieval omission, attention failure and stale knowledge
body: First ask whether the information was saved at all. Then check whether retrieval selected it, whether it reached the prompt, and whether the model used it correctly. A stale answer can arise from old source data even when retrieval succeeds. Each failure needs a different fix; increasing context blindly obscures the cause.

tradeoffs: Sliding window: simple and predictable size; costs include loses early information. Unsafe without durable constraints.
Summarization: condenses history; costs include can distort or omit facts. Needs preservation tests.
Artifact references: keeps exact evidence externally; costs include extra retrieval work. References need availability and authorization.
decisionCriteria: How much tool-result headroom is reserved?
Can the next call recover pending actions?
Which evidence actually reached the prompt?

examples.title: Hypothetical worked example
examples.body: A hypothetical research task has already completed three searches when the context is compacted. Keep completed search IDs, unresolved questions and source references in structured state. Test that the resumed worker does not spend its remaining budget repeating the same searches.

failureModes.symptom: The agent forgets constraints after compaction
failureModes.cause: The summary omitted exact state or early requirements
failureModes.diagnostic: Compare pre/post compaction goal, IDs, approvals and pending actions
failureModes.mitigation: Reload authoritative state and preserve exact constraints outside summaries

verification: Record evidence for: What must remain exact?
Record evidence for: How much tool-result headroom is reserved?
Record evidence for: Can the next call recover pending actions?
Record evidence for: Which evidence actually reached the prompt?
Exercise the failure case: the agent forgets constraints after compaction. Preserve the observed outcome and unresolved limitations.
reconsiderWhen: Context pressure, repeated work or constraint loss

title: Retrieve evidence that is relevant, current and allowed
summary: Choose direct data access or retrieval by the question, then test ingestion, access filtering and answer support separately.

applicability.required: The answer depends on locating evidence outside the current input.
applicability.optional: Use a short evidence review for a small reversible experiment; deepen it as consequences and uncertainty grow.
applicability.unnecessary: A retrieval pipeline is unnecessary when a direct authorized lookup or the supplied input already answers the question.

sections.title: RAG versus direct API/SQL access; RAG versus long context; when neither is required
body: Use authoritative API or SQL access for current structured facts with exact identifiers. Use retrieval for relevant passages across a corpus. Long context can simplify small bounded collections but still needs access control and freshness. If the answer is a deterministic field lookup, neither a vector index nor a model is necessary.

sections.title: Ingestion, parsing/OCR, tables, chunking, embeddings, metadata, indexes
body: Inspect extraction before tuning embeddings. Preserve table headers, page locations, units and document structure through parsing and OCR. Chunk at meaningful boundaries and store source version, access scope and lineage as metadata. Test scans, tables, multilingual content and empty extraction instead of only clean text files.

sections.title: Keyword/vector/hybrid retrieval, reranking, query transformation and access filtering
body: Keyword search preserves exact identifiers; vector search finds semantic similarity; hybrid search combines signals. Reranking adds a second relevance pass with latency and cost. Query rewriting can change intent. Apply access filtering before unauthorized content reaches the model, and test both relevant-item recall and cross-tenant exclusion.

sections.title: Recall/relevance, groundedness, completeness, citation support, conflicting sources
body: Evaluate retrieval and generation separately: did the necessary passages arrive, and did the answer accurately use them? Relevance is not completeness. Check each material claim's citation supports it and flag conflicting sources. Microsoft documents distinct retrieval and answer evaluators; a single groundedness measure cannot prove the entire task is correct.

sections.title: Document updates, deletions, freshness, lineage, authoritative source selection
body: Maintain a mapping from source versions to derived chunks and indexes. Updates should replace superseded records; deletions must propagate to replicas and caches under an explicit policy. Prefer the authoritative current source when documents disagree. A recent ingestion timestamp does not prove the underlying document is current.

alternatives.name: Direct API / SQL
alternatives.benefits: Current structured facts and precise filters
alternatives.limitations: Not suited to broad unstructured discovery

alternatives.name: Long context
alternatives.limitations: Not an access-control or freshness solution

tradeoffs: Direct API / SQL: current structured facts and precise filters; costs include integration and query validation. Not suited to broad unstructured discovery.
Hybrid retrieval: combines exact and semantic matching; costs include index and reranking operations. Recall and permissions need testing.
Long context: simple for a bounded collection; costs include latency and attention cost. Not an access-control or freshness solution.
decisionCriteria: Is the data structured and authoritative?
Did the required passage reach the model?
Does each citation support its claim?

examples.title: Hypothetical worked example
examples.body: A hypothetical shipment-status question should use the current order API. A question about the exceptions in a set of manuals may use document retrieval. Test a scanned table where a number is correct but its unit is dropped; a fluent answer can still be wrong.

examples.title: A small retrieval acceptance set
examples.body: Hypothetical fixtures: Q1 asks a current order status and must use the order API; Q2 asks a policy exception and needs page 4 of policy v2; Q3 asks for a deleted document and must not retrieve its old chunks; Q4 uses a similar title in another tenant and must return no unauthorized passage; Q5 asks a table value whose unit crosses a page break. For each, record extracted text, expected evidence IDs, retrieved evidence IDs, authorization result and answer citations. Fix extraction before reranking if Q5 lost its unit.

failureModes.cause: Extraction or retrieval omitted necessary evidence
failureModes.diagnostic: Inspect parsed source, selected chunks and claim-to-citation support
failureModes.mitigation: Repair the earliest failing stage and re-evaluate final answers

verification: Record evidence for: Is the data structured and authoritative?
Record evidence for: Was extraction correct?
Record evidence for: Did the required passage reach the model?
Record evidence for: Does each citation support its claim?
Exercise the failure case: the answer is plausible but incomplete. Preserve the observed outcome and unresolved limitations.
reconsiderWhen: Source changes, missing citations or retrieval drift

title: Memory versus RAG: decide what should persist
summary: Separate execution state, conversation, reusable memory and business facts. Give remembered information a correction and deletion path.

applicability.required: Information must be remembered across tasks or sessions for a defined purpose.
applicability.optional: Use a short evidence review for a small reversible experiment; deepen it as consequences and uncertainty grow.
applicability.unnecessary: Long-term memory is unnecessary when each task can be completed from its current inputs. Execution state may still be needed.

prerequisites: Identity namespaces and a write policy

sections.title: Execution state versus conversation versus long-term memory versus business database
body: Execution state tracks what happened in a workflow; conversation stores interaction history; long-term memory stores selected reusable context; the business database owns business facts. Keep these roles explicit. Do not reconstruct whether a payment occurred from a conversation summary when a transaction ledger exists.

sections.title: Semantic facts/preferences, episodic examples, procedural guidance
body: Semantic memory represents facts or preferences, episodic memory records prior examples, and procedural memory describes how to do something. Choose the type based on the future query. Keep a preference separate from an instruction granting authority. A past successful action is evidence of history, not permission to repeat it.

sections.title: Explicit/inferred memory writes, synchronous/background writes, approval of sensitive changes
body: Require an explicit write policy: which facts can be inferred, who can correct them and which sensitive changes require approval. Synchronous writes offer immediate availability; background writes reduce request latency but may lag or fail. Record provenance and make user-visible corrections possible rather than silently treating an inference as fact.

sections.title: Namespaces, provenance, confidence limitations, deduplication, contradictions
body: Namespace memories by the identity and purpose that may use them. Store where a claim came from, when it was observed and what supersedes it. A confidence number is not calibrated truth unless measured. Deduplicate cautiously: two similar statements may concern different entities or different dates.

sections.title: TTL, correction, deletion propagation, retention, poisoning, stale assumptions
body: Set retention and expiry according to purpose. Corrections should supersede wrong records and invalidate derived summaries; deletions need a propagation policy. Test poisoned writes from untrusted documents and stale assumptions after a user changes preferences. Critical policy and permissions must be read from their authoritative control system.

sections.title: Relational/key-value/vector/graph storage choices, driven by access patterns
body: Use relational storage for constraints and joins, key-value storage for exact lookup, vectors for semantic similarity and graphs for relationship traversal. Combining stores can help but adds consistency work. Start from access patterns and deletion requirements; do not choose a vector database merely because the product uses AI.

sections.title: Memory is not automatic learning or truth; critical permissions are not conversational memories
body: Memory changes future context, not the model's learned weights, and can preserve mistakes as easily as useful facts. Validate important recalled information against authoritative data. Memory is optional for stateless tasks; durable execution state is a separate need. Never store a reusable authorization decision as a conversational preference.

tradeoffs: No long-term memory: simplest retention and isolation; costs include repeated setup by users. Does not provide personalization.
Structured key-value facts: exact retrieval and updates; costs include requires explicit schema. Poor for fuzzy discovery.
Vector memory: semantic lookup; costs include relevance and deletion complexity. Similarity is not truth.
Graph memory: relationship queries; costs include schema and consistency work. Unnecessary without relationship needs.
decisionCriteria: Is this state, evidence or preference?
Who may write and correct it?
How do deletions reach derived stores?

examples.title: Hypothetical worked example
examples.body: A hypothetical assistant remembers a preferred report format. That preference can shape a draft, but cannot authorize sending it. Store the preference with provenance and correction controls; load current send permissions from the access-control system.

examples.title: A correction record
examples.body: Hypothetical preference: project=A, user=U, key=report_format, value=PDF, provenance=explicit user request, observedAt=t1. At t2 the user requests HTML. Store the correction as superseding the old value, invalidate derived summaries/caches and verify the next retrieval returns HTML under the same namespace. A similar preference in project B is untouched. Retention/deletion policy must describe when both the current and superseded records disappear. This preference cannot grant permission to send a report.

failureModes.symptom: An old preference overrides a correction
failureModes.cause: Derived memory or caches were not invalidated
failureModes.diagnostic: Trace provenance, supersession and retrieval namespace for the recalled value
failureModes.mitigation: Correct the source record and propagate invalidation; verify future retrieval

verification: Record evidence for: Is this state, evidence or preference?
Record evidence for: Who may write and correct it?
Record evidence for: When does it expire?
Record evidence for: How do deletions reach derived stores?
Exercise the failure case: an old preference overrides a correction. Preserve the observed outcome and unresolved limitations.
reconsiderWhen: Preference correction, retention changes or poisoned memory

title: Design tools that are safe to choose and verify
summary: Make tool intent clear, validate business arguments and report externally verified outcomes.

applicability.required: A model selects or supplies arguments to an API, database, browser or code tool.
applicability.optional: Use a short evidence review for a small reversible experiment; deepen it as consequences and uncertainty grow.
applicability.unnecessary: Do not implement every pattern here. Omit mechanisms that do not address an identified requirement, and record the rationale.

prerequisites: A classification of read and write effects

sections.title: Names, descriptions, schemas, non-overlap, discovery, restricted tool sets
body: Name tools by the business action they perform and distinguish similar operations with clear scope and examples. Use schemas with precise units and identifiers. Expose a restricted set relevant to the task; dynamic discovery still needs policy filtering. Evaluate selection errors, not just whether the endpoint works when called manually.

sections.title: Fine-grained wrappers versus business operations; ergonomics and tool-choice evaluation
body: Fine-grained wrappers are reusable but force the model to coordinate many calls. A business operation can enforce invariants in one place, but may be too broad if its effects are unclear. Offer a preview for compound actions. Test ambiguous requests against competing tools and inspect why the wrong one was selected.

sections.title: Argument validation, identifiers, ownership, preconditions and postconditions
body: Validate arguments structurally and semantically, including caller ownership, entity existence, units, limits and current preconditions. Perform authorization at dispatch time, not only when listing tools. Check postconditions against external state. Reject unknown identifiers rather than allowing the model to invent a new target.

sections.title: Dispatch, sequential/parallel calls, pagination, bounded results and useful errors
body: Parallelize independent reads; serialize dependent actions unless concurrency semantics are explicit. Bound pagination and response size and return continuation tokens. Errors should distinguish invalid input, denied access, transient failure and unknown outcome. Include enough evidence to recover without leaking secrets or prompting blind retries.

sections.title: Read versus write tools, dry-run/preview, approval-bound exact actions
body: Classify tools as read, draft or write and make side effects visible. Bind approval to exact parameters, target, identity, scope and expiry. A dry run must genuinely avoid writes; label limitations if it cannot guarantee the final result. Revalidate the approved action against current state before execution.

sections.title: API/database contracts, external outcome verification and reconciliation
body: Design contracts with versioning, idempotency and queryable operation IDs where possible. Treat a timeout after dispatch as an uncertain outcome until reconciled. A successful HTTP code may only mean accepted for processing; verify the business postcondition before saying the work completed.

sections.title: MCP suitability versus direct integration; protocols do not replace authorization
body: MCP standardizes an integration interface; it does not decide whether your application should authorize an action. Direct integration may be simpler for one stable API, while MCP can serve multiple clients. Check transport authentication, token audience, server identity and permissions independently of the model's tool instructions.

sections.title: Dependency hygiene, testable boundaries, coding standards, reviews
body: Keep dependencies pinned and review lockfile changes, transitive packages and maintenance responsibilities. Isolate provider and tool adapters for contract testing. Require readable errors, bounded resources and safe logging in review. Generated code needs the same scrutiny as human code and should be understandable during an incident.

sections.title: Review AI-generated code and claims; avoid unnecessary frameworks, agents and abstractions
body: Inspect AI-generated changes against the actual request and run checks that exercise real behavior. Reject invented test claims and abstraction added without a concrete need. Compare dependency cost with a direct implementation. A passing test that merely repeats the implementation's assumptions does not establish the business requirement.

sections.title: Clear documentation and examples; implementation must remain understandable by another engineer
body: Document a successful call, an invalid call, a denied call and recovery from an uncertain result. Include units, identifiers, ownership and expected postconditions. Another engineer should be able to operate the integration without reverse-engineering a prompt. Keep examples hypothetical and free of real credentials or private payloads.

tradeoffs: Fine-grained tools: composable and reusable; costs include more calls and coordination. Can expose invalid intermediate actions.
Business operation tool: centralizes invariants; costs include larger operation contract. Effects must remain understandable.
Direct integration: simple for one api; costs include client-specific adapter. Less reusable across clients.
MCP integration: common discovery and invocation surface; costs include server lifecycle and trust. Does not replace authorization.
decisionCriteria: Can a human distinguish competing tools?

examples.title: Hypothetical worked example
examples.body: A hypothetical update-address tool requires customer ID, address, expected record version and operation key. It verifies ownership and the record version before writing. If the network fails after dispatch, the caller queries the operation rather than assuming nothing happened.

examples.title: A tool contract and its approval record
examples.body: Hypothetical send_report input: projectId:string, reportId:string, recipientId:string, expectedReportVersion:integer, operationId:string. Domain checks: caller owns project; report belongs to project; recipient is permitted; version matches; operation ID has not been used for different parameters. Approval record: action=send_report, parametersHash=<hash of canonical validated input>, approverId, approvedAt, expiresAt, policyVersion. Dispatch compares the exact hash and current authority. Result is one of rejected, accepted(operationId), verified(providerMessageId), or outcome_unknown(operationId). Never return verified merely because dispatch returned HTTP 202.

failureModes.symptom: The tool reports success but the task is unfinished
failureModes.cause: Acceptance by an API was confused with the business postcondition
failureModes.diagnostic: Query operation status and inspect the actual target record
failureModes.mitigation: Keep the result pending or outcome unknown until verification completes

verification: Record evidence for: Can a human distinguish competing tools?
Record evidence for: Are IDs and ownership checked?
Record evidence for: What does success actually mean?
Record evidence for: How are uncertain writes reconciled?
Exercise the failure case: the tool reports success but the task is unfinished. Preserve the observed outcome and unresolved limitations.
reconsiderWhen: New tools, schema changes or selection errors

title: Recover without duplicating business actions
summary: Design for crashes, retries and unknown outcomes. Durable state does not make external effects exactly once.

applicability.required: Work can outlive a request, be retried, recover after a crash or change external state.
applicability.optional: Use a short evidence review for a small reversible experiment; deepen it as consequences and uncertainty grow.
applicability.unnecessary: Do not implement every pattern here. Omit mechanisms that do not address an identified requirement, and record the rationale.

prerequisites: Queryable operation IDs or reconciliation plan

sections.title: Connection/read/overall deadlines; retry classification and retry ownership
body: Set distinct connection, per-attempt and overall deadlines. Classify errors by whether retrying is useful and safe; validation and authorization errors normally need a changed request. Decide which layer owns retries so SDK, worker and orchestrator policies do not multiply attempts without a common limit.

sections.title: Backoff/jitter, retry budgets, circuit breakers, dependency isolation
body: Use backoff with jitter for transient retryable failures and bound attempts by the remaining task deadline and budget. Circuit breakers can reduce repeated pressure on unhealthy dependencies. Isolate pools so one stalled service cannot consume all workers. AWS guidance emphasizes choosing the retry layer and checking idempotency.

sections.title: Idempotency, unknown outcomes after timeout, outbox/inbox, deduplication
body: Generate a stable operation key before dispatch and persist intent. If the call times out, query its status or reconcile before resending. Use outbox/inbox patterns for coordinating local state and message processing. Deduplication retention must cover the retry horizon; it cannot remove duplicate effects already executed downstream.

sections.title: Checkpoints, replay versus fresh rerun, side-effect boundaries
body: Checkpoint durable facts and separate replayable computation from external side effects. A replay reconstructs an execution from recorded history; a fresh rerun can issue new actions. Verify the chosen runtime's behavior with a controlled crash immediately before and after an external call. Persist the operation identity across recovery.

sections.title: Queue limits, duplicate/out-of-order events, dead letters, backpressure
body: Bound queue length, age and concurrency. Expect duplicate and out-of-order events; use business keys and version checks. Dead letters need an owner and safe replay instructions, not an unattended pile. Apply backpressure or reject work when accepting more would violate deadlines or available review capacity.

sections.title: Heartbeat versus real progress, watchdogs, repeated-action detection
body: A heartbeat proves a worker is alive, not that the task is advancing. Measure progress through verified milestones or new evidence. Detect repeated action signatures and unchanged outputs. A watchdog should first stop further side effects, capture state and escalate; restarting a live but confused loop may simply repeat the problem.

sections.title: Worker leases/ownership and fencing stale workers; safe reassignment
body: A lease grants temporary ownership, but a paused worker may resume after its lease expires. Use fencing tokens or version checks at the write boundary to reject stale workers. Safe reassignment requires both a new owner and protection against the old owner's late writes.

sections.title: Cancellation, graceful shutdown, resource cleanup, bounded delegation
body: Cancellation needs an explicit state and propagation to child tasks, queued jobs and in-flight operations. Graceful shutdown stops new work and checkpoints safe state. Some external actions cannot be cancelled; reconcile them and report their final outcome. Cleanup should be idempotent and bounded.

sections.title: Approval timeouts, stale approvals, revalidation of current business state
body: Approvals expire when their time limit or relevant business assumptions change. On resume, compare the approved parameters and entity version with current state. A person approving a price yesterday does not authorize a different price today. Expired approvals return to review rather than silently being renewed.

sections.title: Recovery, compensation, manual fallback, restore/reconciliation procedures
body: Define recovery per state: retry a safe read, reconcile an unknown write, compensate a completed action if valid, or hand off manually. Compensation can fail and needs its own audit trail. Keep a tested restore procedure that includes business reconciliation, not only a successful database restore.

sections.title: Fault injection, worker-kill tests, dependency outages and duplicate-action checks
body: Inject failure at meaningful boundaries: kill a worker after remote success but before checkpoint, duplicate an event, delay an API and remove a dependency. Assert business invariants and the absence of duplicate actions. Test recovery with realistic permissions and disposable fixtures, then record actual observed behavior.

sections.title: No promise of exactly-once external effects merely because execution is durable
body: Durable execution helps retain state and resume work; it does not make arbitrary external systems execute exactly once. State the guarantee at each boundary and its assumptions. When the downstream service lacks deduplication or status lookup, retain an explicit uncertain state and a manual reconciliation path.

tradeoffs: Fresh rerun: easy for pure computation; costs include repeats work. Unsafe for untracked side effects.
Checkpoint and resume: retains progress; costs include state and versioning work. Needs explicit effect boundaries.
Manual reconciliation: handles ambiguous external outcomes; costs include human time and delay. Requires usable evidence and ownership.
decisionCriteria: Can a stale worker still act?
What evidence proves progress and completion?

examples.title: Hypothetical worked example
examples.body: A hypothetical notification provider accepts a send, but the response is lost. The worker must retain an outcome-unknown state and query by operation ID. Restarting from the beginning with a new ID may send a second notification. Test this exact boundary in a disposable environment.

examples.title: Ambiguous timeout: failed and corrected recovery
examples.body: Hypothetical trace: 10:00:00 persist intent op-42; 10:00:01 provider accepts op-42; 10:00:02 connection drops; 10:00:03 worker dies. Failed recovery creates op-43 and sends again. Corrected recovery reloads op-42 as outcome unknown, queries the provider, records its message ID and verifies the recipient. If status lookup is unavailable, stop automatic retries and assign reconciliation. If confirmed not sent, retry only under the documented same-key semantics. Test both crashes: after remote acceptance and after local confirmation.

failureModes.cause: A timed-out write was repeated with no stable operation key
failureModes.diagnostic: Correlate operation IDs, provider state and checkpoint timing
failureModes.mitigation: Stop retries, reconcile external state and resume with deduplication or manual handling

verification: Record evidence for: Who owns retries?
Record evidence for: Can the write be deduplicated?
Record evidence for: Can a stale worker still act?
Record evidence for: What evidence proves progress and completion?
Exercise the failure case: recovery duplicates a business action. Preserve the observed outcome and unresolved limitations.
reconsiderWhen: Worker crashes, duplicated actions or rising retry rates

title: Keep authority outside the model
summary: Constrain identity, actions and data access; make approval and incident ownership concrete.

applicability.required: The system handles nonpublic data, reaches external tools or affects other people.
applicability.optional: Use a short evidence review for a small reversible experiment; deepen it as consequences and uncertainty grow.
applicability.unnecessary: Do not implement every pattern here. Omit mechanisms that do not address an identified requirement, and record the rationale.

sections.title: Risk assessment, workflow inventory, action boundaries, abuse cases
body: Inventory the workflow's data, tools, actors and potential consequences. Threat-model both accidental misuse and deliberate abuse, including valid credentials used for an invalid purpose. Write an action boundary for each tool. Risk depends on the reachable business effect, not whether the interface looks like a friendly chat.

sections.title: Prompt injection, untrusted tools/documents, poisoned memory, exfiltration
body: Treat retrieved text, tool responses and memory as untrusted data that can contain instructions. An attacker may try to redirect the task, poison future context or extract secrets. Enforce permissions and outbound destinations outside the model. Test malicious documents alongside ordinary ones; filtering alone is not a complete defense.

sections.title: Identity, delegated authority, least privilege, tenant isolation and secrets
body: Run under a defined identity with narrowly scoped, short-lived credentials where supported. Verify tenant ownership at every resource access and keep secrets out of prompts and logs. Delegating a task does not automatically delegate all of the parent's authority. Test denial across similar IDs in different tenants.

sections.title: Connector provenance, MCP authentication/authorization, supply-chain changes
body: Verify connector publisher, package integrity, endpoint identity and update behavior. Review MCP authentication and authorization independently; discoverable tools still need access checks. A changed schema or dependency may broaden reachable actions. Pin or review updates and maintain an inventory of connectors with responsible owners.

sections.title: Sandboxing, filesystem/network/egress restrictions for code/browser agents
body: Isolate code and browser execution with filesystem, network and process limits appropriate to the task. Restrict egress and credential availability; an untrusted script should not inherit production secrets. Containers provide useful boundaries but need correct configuration. Do not expose a host Docker socket to agent-controlled code.

sections.title: Approval controls bound to exact action; revocation and time-of-check/time-of-use
body: Show the exact proposed effect to the approver and bind approval to immutable action details and an expiry. Check authorization again at execution to handle revocation and changed state. If parameters change after approval, obtain a new decision. Logging 'approved' without the approved object is weak evidence.

sections.title: Input/output handling, retention, data minimization, log redaction
body: Minimize collected data and define retention separately for prompts, traces, exports and indexes. Redact sensitive values before logging. Treat generated content as untrusted when rendering HTML, opening URLs or executing commands. An internal interface can still leak data through logs, browser storage or third-party error reporting.

sections.title: Fairness, accessibility, explainability, appeals where decisions affect people
body: When outputs affect people, define who can challenge them and how errors are corrected. Test relevant segments and accessibility of review interfaces. Explain the evidence and limitations in language the user understands. Human oversight must have time, authority and information to disagree, rather than merely click approval.

sections.title: Applicability of company policy/legal review; no invented compliance certification
body: Identify applicable organizational policy and obtain qualified legal or domain review when the use case requires it. This playbook provides engineering guidance and does not certify compliance. Record unresolved applicability questions and the responsible reviewer; do not turn a generic checklist into a legal conclusion.

sections.title: Business/process owner, engineering owner, security/domain reviewer, budget owner, operations owner, release authority
body: Name the process owner for outcomes, engineering owner for implementation, security/domain reviewer for risk, budget owner for spending, operations owner for incidents and release authority for launch. State who can halt the system. A role without a person or escalation path is an unresolved operating requirement.

sections.title: One startup employee may hold multiple roles, but responsibilities remain named
body: In a small team one person can hold several roles, but list each responsibility separately to expose conflicts and gaps. Higher-impact changes may warrant an independent reviewer even when staffing is limited. Record accepted residual risk and who accepted it; silence is not approval.

sections.title: Governance aligned with Govern/Map/Measure/Manage as guidance, not blanket legal obligation
body: NIST's AI RMF organizes risk work through Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. Use that structure to connect ownership, context, evidence and treatment decisions. Its use here is voluntary guidance rather than a claim that every project has the same legal duties or that completing it confers certification.

sections.title: Incident ownership, escalation, release/increased-autonomy approval, shutdown
body: Prepare a named incident path: who receives the alert, who can disable actions, who reconciles effects and who communicates with affected users. Treat increased autonomy as a new release decision. Exercise revocation and shutdown under realistic conditions, including child tasks already running.

sections.title: Independent review proportionate to impact and accepted residual risk
body: Match independent review to consequence, uncertainty and reversibility. Give reviewers the actual evidence, exclusions and operating limits. Record accepted residual risks and revisit triggers. Approval of a narrow pilot should not quietly become approval for a broader population, new tools or a larger action budget.

tradeoffs: Read-only assistance: smaller action surface; costs include user performs final work. Still handles sensitive data.
Exact-action approval: human checks a defined effect; costs include review staffing and fatigue. Stale approvals need revalidation.
Bounded autonomy: less routine review; costs include stronger enforcement and monitoring. Requires explicit risk acceptance.
decisionCriteria: What can this identity actually do?
Can untrusted text reach a write path?
Who can stop and reconcile the system?

examples.title: Hypothetical worked example
examples.body: A hypothetical retrieved document tells the assistant to upload its credentials. The runtime must prevent secret access and unapproved egress even if the model follows that text. Approval for a report draft does not authorize running commands from the document.

examples.title: Confused deputy: an allowed reader and an allowed sender
examples.body: Hypothetical attack: a retrieved ticket tells the assistant to read a confidential file and email it to a new address. The connector is authenticated, but that does not make the document authoritative. Enforce caller-and-object authorization on the read, minimize data exposed to the worker, and apply destination/data policy on the send. The approval screen must display the real recipient and content scope, not a model-written assurance. Record the rejected operation and source ID. If data already left, disable further sends and follow incident reconciliation. Destination allowlists alone do not prevent leaks to an allowed recipient; review information flow and residual risk.

failureModes.cause: Instructions in tool results crossed the policy boundary
failureModes.diagnostic: Inspect the source, proposed action and dispatch authorization decision
failureModes.mitigation: Disable the unsafe action path, revoke scope if needed and enforce policy outside the model

verification: Record evidence for: What can this identity actually do?
Record evidence for: Can untrusted text reach a write path?
Record evidence for: What exactly was approved?
Record evidence for: Who can stop and reconcile the system?
Exercise the failure case: untrusted evidence redirects an action. Preserve the observed outcome and unresolved limitations.
