title: Build evidence that a task works
summary: Measure outcomes and invariants with representative cases, calibrated graders and repeated runs.

applicability.required: You need evidence to compare approaches, release a change or investigate quality.
applicability.optional: Use a short evidence review for a small reversible experiment; deepen it as consequences and uncertainty grow.
applicability.unnecessary: Do not implement every pattern here. Omit mechanisms that do not address an identified requirement, and record the rationale.

prerequisites: Acceptance criteria with a ground-truth owner

sections.title: Acceptance criteria, ground-truth owner, uncertainty and disagreement resolution
body: Define success with someone who owns the domain outcome. Record ambiguous cases and the procedure for resolving disagreement instead of forcing an arbitrary label. Acceptance thresholds need a denominator, sampling method and consequence model. Separate facts that can be checked from subjective quality preferences.

sections.title: Unit, integration, contract, end-to-end, load, security and failure tests
body: Use unit tests for deterministic policy, contract tests for adapters, integration tests for boundaries and end-to-end tests for outcomes. Add load, security and failure tests where their risks exist. Model evaluations complement these layers; they do not replace authorization tests or a restore drill.

sections.title: Representative cases, holdouts, dataset versions, contamination and overfitting
body: Build cases from the intended task distribution, including rare important failures and realistic messy inputs. Version the dataset and reserve a holdout set not used during prompt tuning. Track where examples came from. Repeatedly optimizing against the same visible cases can improve a benchmark while harming general behavior.

sections.title: Code graders, model judges, human review, rubric design and judge calibration
body: Use code graders for exact invariants and known answers, human review for nuanced judgments, and model judges when a calibrated rubric makes them useful. Compare judges with independently labeled examples and inspect disagreements. Hide irrelevant presentation cues and test whether verbosity or confident tone biases scores.

sections.title: Outcome versus trajectory evaluation; allow valid alternate paths while enforcing invariants
body: Judge the business end state and also enforce required process constraints, such as no unauthorized writes. Allow different valid tool paths when they satisfy the contract. A trace that looks reasonable can end with no completed transaction; a correct answer can still have leaked data while producing it.

sections.title: Repeated runs, reliability distributions, sampling uncertainty and rare severe failures
body: Run variable tasks repeatedly and report the distribution of success, latency and cost. A single successful attempt is not a reliability estimate. Confidence intervals and sample size matter, especially for rare severe errors. If no severe failure appears in a small sample, report the limited evidence instead of zero risk.

sections.title: Segment results by task difficulty, language, document type and consequence
body: Break results down by task difficulty, language, document quality, customer segment where appropriate, and consequence. An aggregate can hide a harmful weak subgroup. Keep enough cases per segment to avoid overinterpreting noise. Choose release gates that reflect the actual users and risks.

sections.title: Component evals for retrieval, memory, routing, tools, context and delegation
body: Test retrieval recall, memory correction, route selection, tool arguments, context preservation and delegation separately. Component checks help locate causes; an integrated outcome test catches interactions. A retrieval improvement that increases irrelevant context may worsen the final answer, so measure both levels.

sections.title: Hallucinated facts/IDs/recommendations/completion claims and distinct checks
body: Check factual claims against evidence, IDs against authoritative records, recommendations against constraints and completion claims against external state. These are different error classes. A grounded paragraph can still recommend the wrong action. A valid schema proves the shape of output, not the truth of its contents.

sections.title: Abstention and escalation evaluation; false positives versus false negatives
body: Include tasks where the correct behavior is to abstain, request information or escalate. Measure unnecessary escalation as well as unsafe action. False positives and false negatives often have different consequences. Verify that escalation arrives with enough context for a person to resolve it efficiently.

sections.title: Low temperature, RAG, valid JSON or another model's agreement are not guarantees
body: Low temperature may reduce variability but does not establish correctness. Retrieval can supply wrong or incomplete evidence. JSON validation cannot check truth, and another model can repeat the same error. Combine independent evidence and deterministic checks with calibrated human judgment according to the task.

sections.title: Isolated test environments, resets, safe fixtures, no production side effects
body: Use isolated environments, fake recipients, disposable records and resettable fixtures. Confirm tool credentials cannot reach production writes. Each run should begin from a known state so previous outcomes do not contaminate results. Validate the test harness itself with deliberately incorrect outputs and known-good examples.

sections.title: Regression gates, sensitivity to real failures, production sampling
body: Gate changes against representative regressions and severe invariants, then sample production quality with privacy controls. Test that the suite detects a known bad prompt, tool or model version. A test that passes everything cannot protect a release. Add real incident cases after review and de-identification.

sections.title: Attribute failures to model, context, tools, runtime, data or test
body: Trace a failure through input data, assembled context, model output, policy decision, tool result and grader. Distinguish model limitations from tool bugs and bad labels. Preserve versions and reproducible fixtures. Fixing the wrong layer often increases cost without addressing the failure users experienced.

sections.title: Evaluate full business outcomes including external state and review/rework
body: Measure whether the complete business task succeeded after review, retries and rework. Anthropic distinguishes transcripts from final environment outcomes in its evaluation guidance. For a hypothetical ticket workflow, inspect the correct ticket state and recipient, not only the agent saying 'done'. Keep completion evidence alongside the run.

tradeoffs: Code graders: exact repeatable assertions; costs include need formal expected properties. Miss nuanced quality.
Model judges: scales rubric-based assessment; costs include judge bias and cost. Must be calibrated.
Human review: domain nuance and discovery; costs include time and disagreement. Sampling and consistency limits.
decisionCriteria: Does the grader catch a known failure?

examples.title: Hypothetical worked example
examples.body: A hypothetical booking assistant produces a persuasive confirmation, but no booking exists. Grade both the final response and the reservation table, verify the correct user and ensure no duplicate booking. Include cases that should request clarification and cases where tools fail.

examples.title: A usable evaluation report template
examples.body: Hypothetical report, not a benchmark: dataset v3 has 200 independently sampled cases; 180 verified outcomes pass, so observed success is 90%. Report a binomial interval with its method (for example Wilson), rather than reporting 90% as exact reliability. If zero severe failures are observed, the rough rule-of-three upper bound is 3/200=1.5% at approximately 95% confidence under independent representative trials; clustered or biased samples weaken that interpretation. Report language/document segments with their own denominators. Compare old and new versions on the same cases, list improved/regressed pairs, and review disagreements. Record human label disagreements and their adjudication. Release depends on consequence-specific thresholds and unresolved severe cases, not this illustrative percentage.

failureModes.symptom: Offline evaluations pass but users report poor quality
failureModes.cause: Cases, graders or segments miss the production failure
failureModes.diagnostic: Reproduce the report with its configuration and inspect grader sensitivity
failureModes.mitigation: Pause expansion, add a reviewed regression and fix the responsible component

verification: Record evidence for: Does the grader catch a known failure?
Record evidence for: Is the holdout untouched?
Record evidence for: Which segments perform poorly?
Record evidence for: Was external state checked?
Exercise the failure case: offline evaluations pass but users report poor quality. Preserve the observed outcome and unresolved limitations.
reconsiderWhen: New model, prompt, tools, task mix or incidents

title: Budget for verified outcomes, not cheap calls
summary: Include retries, review, queues and shared agent budgets in cost and capacity decisions.

applicability.required: The workflow consumes metered resources, has capacity limits or needs budget approval.
applicability.optional: Use a short evidence review for a small reversible experiment; deepen it as consequences and uncertainty grow.
applicability.unnecessary: Do not implement every pattern here. Omit mechanisms that do not address an identified requirement, and record the rationale.

sections.title: Total cost per verified successful task, including failures and human review
body: Use total operating cost divided by verified successful tasks, with a defined reporting period. Include failed attempts and human review in the numerator. If no tasks succeed, cost per success is undefined rather than zero. Compare with the manual or conventional baseline using the same outcome definition.

sections.title: Models, input/output tokens, caching, embeddings, retrieval, tools, infrastructure and observability
body: Account for input and output tokens, cached usage, embeddings, retrieval, tool fees, compute, storage and observability. Prices and billing units vary, so enter current contracted values explicitly. A model-only estimate misses integration and labor. Keep forecast assumptions separate from measured bills.

sections.title: Latency distribution, throughput, concurrency and queue wait; not averages alone
body: Measure p50, p95 and p99 latency where sample size supports them, plus queue wait and end-to-end completion. Throughput is completed work per time; concurrency is work in progress. More concurrency can increase throttling and tail latency. Test realistic bursts and slow dependencies before sizing capacity.

sections.title: Attribution per workflow/project/tenant/model/tool
body: Attach cost and usage to workflow, project, tenant, model, tool and operation IDs. Reconcile estimates with billing records when available. Avoid logging private prompt content merely to attribute costs. Missing attribution should appear as unknown spend rather than being silently allocated to a convenient bucket.

sections.title: Concurrency-safe budget reservations and reconciliation with billed usage
body: Reserve budget atomically before starting concurrent work, then reconcile against observed usage and release unused reservations. Otherwise several workers can each see the same remaining balance and overspend. Define how to account for unknown usage after a timeout and maintain a conservative reserve for in-flight work.

sections.title: Shared parent/child/retry budgets; limits on calls, output, time and delegation
body: Give the root task a shared budget covering children and retries, plus limits on calls, output size, wall time and delegation. A child limit alone does not constrain total tree cost. Retain enough budget for verification and a useful final handoff rather than exhausting everything on exploration.

sections.title: Delayed billing and in-flight requests; alerts are not hard spending caps
body: Billing may arrive late and a cancelled request may still be charged. Alerts notify; they are not necessarily enforceable caps. Apply admission control using estimates and safety margin, and document the residual overshoot risk. Do not promise an exact spending ceiling that the provider cannot enforce.

sections.title: Quotas, forecasts, budget exhaustion behaviour, load shedding and escalation
body: Define behavior before capacity or budget is exhausted: queue within a deadline, reject, downgrade through a validated path, or escalate. Forecast using expected and stress scenarios, not only average volume. Rate limits, human-review capacity and downstream quotas can be tighter than model capacity.

sections.title: Validated cheaper fallback, batching, cache correctness/freshness/isolation
body: Validate cheaper fallback quality before routing live work. Batch only when latency requirements allow it. Cache keys need task-relevant inputs, configuration versions and authorization scope; expire or invalidate stale answers. A cross-tenant or stale cache hit is a correctness failure, even if it saves tokens.

sections.title: Model quality/cost trade-offs; cheap calls may create more retries and rework
body: A cheap model can cost more per outcome if it creates retries, escalations or rework. Compare total task cost and quality under the same workload and constraints. Use a small routing experiment with clear stop conditions. Do not infer the best production choice from price per token alone.

sections.title: Avoid buying capacity before value is demonstrated
body: Confirm useful demand and measurable value before buying reserved capacity or adding infrastructure. Optimize the dominant measured cost first. Removing an unnecessary step or improving tool results may outperform a model upgrade. Include the engineering time spent optimizing a low-volume workflow in the decision.

sections.title: Estimation calculators with explicit user inputs, units and assumptions; no invented live prices
body: Use calculators as scenario tools with explicit volume, calls, token counts, unit prices, review minutes, labor rate, fixed costs and success rate. State units and whether failed attempts are already included. Show assumptions and undefined cases clearly. Estimates are not live quotes, invoices or guaranteed savings.

alternatives.name: Cheaper model
alternatives.limitations: Must pass the same task gates

tradeoffs: Cheaper model: lower unit price; costs include potential rework and retries. Must pass the same task gates.
Batching: can reduce scheduling overhead; costs include adds waiting. Unsuitable for tight interactive deadlines.
Caching: avoids repeated work; costs include invalidation and isolation. Stale results can be harmful.
Fewer steps: reduces work directly; costs include may reduce quality. Validate outcome before removing checks.
decisionCriteria: What is the cost per verified success?

examples.title: Hypothetical worked example
examples.body: A hypothetical workflow costs 100 units for 100 attempts, but only 50 pass review. Its automated cost per verified success is 2 units before labor and infrastructure. Reducing per-call price while doubling rework may be a poor trade. Enter your own prices in the calculator.

examples.title: A cost scenario with review labor
examples.body: Hypothetical month: 1,000 attempts, 800 verified successes, 80 currency units in model/tool usage, 40 in infrastructure and 10 hours of review at 30/hour. Total cost is 420; cost per verified success is 420/800=0.525 currency units. Include failed attempts in the 1,000 rather than multiplying their cost twice. If no successes occur, the metric is undefined. Compare the same business outcomes and review quality with the baseline. Prices here are invented example inputs, not provider quotes.

failureModes.symptom: Cost and queue latency rise together
failureModes.cause: Unbounded retries or concurrency amplify a slow dependency
failureModes.diagnostic: Inspect per-task attempts, in-flight work, queue age and verified success
failureModes.mitigation: Limit admission and retries, preserve useful state and escalate exhausted jobs

verification: Record evidence for: What is the cost per verified success?
Record evidence for: Are retries already included?
Record evidence for: How are concurrent budgets reserved?
Record evidence for: What happens at exhaustion?
Exercise the failure case: cost and queue latency rise together. Preserve the observed outcome and unresolved limitations.
reconsiderWhen: Usage mix, rates, review demand or latency changes

title: Release with a recovery path
summary: Connect deployment, quality evidence, operating ownership and reversible rollout.

applicability.required: A system is being piloted, deployed, upgraded or operated for real users.
applicability.optional: Use a short evidence review for a small reversible experiment; deepen it as consequences and uncertainty grow.
applicability.unnecessary: Do not implement every pattern here. Omit mechanisms that do not address an identified requirement, and record the rationale.

prerequisites: A tested rollback and manual fallback

sections.title: Production operating contract: allowed actions, completion evidence, limits, owner
body: Write an operating contract that names allowed actions, completion evidence, maximum resource use, owner and fallback. Include what the system must refuse and when a person takes over. Make the contract visible to developers and operators so reliability is measured against business behavior, not merely server uptime.

sections.title: Release evidence pack with risk-appropriate requirements and known gaps
body: Assemble release evidence: acceptance results, representative failures, security review, recovery tests, budget behavior and unresolved risks. The release authority should see exclusions and manual duties. Checklist coverage describes review work; it does not certify a system as production-safe.

sections.title: Shadow execution without writes, pilots, staged release and stop conditions
body: Start with shadow execution that cannot write, then a limited pilot and staged expansion. Define eligible traffic, monitoring, review staffing and stop conditions before launch. Compare outcomes with the existing process. A shadow system still handles data, so its access and retention need appropriate controls.

sections.title: Version prompts/models/tools/indexes/memory policy/workflow/evaluation datasets
body: Version prompts, models, tool contracts, retrieval indexes, memory policy, workflow code and evaluation datasets together in a release manifest. Record actual configuration per run. Without this, a quality regression may be impossible to attribute. A model alias can change independently, so track provider notices too.

sections.title: In-flight upgrades, compatible state migration, old-version drain or parallel versions
body: Decide how in-flight jobs survive upgrades: compatible migration, draining old workers or parallel versions. Test restoring old checkpoints with the intended code. Do not resume a historical action under a new policy silently. Keep rollback artifacts and know which state changes cannot be reversed.

sections.title: Traces tied to business IDs with redaction; logs, metrics and decision evidence
body: Connect traces to business operation IDs and configuration versions. Capture important state transitions, validation results, timings and completion evidence with redaction. Limit access and retention. Logging everything may expose private data and still fail to explain which external action actually occurred.

sections.title: Quality/progress objectives alongside availability; correct HTTP does not mean correct work
body: Monitor useful progress and verified task outcomes alongside availability, queue age and latency. A service returning HTTP 200 can repeatedly choose the wrong tool. Define quality alerts based on reviewed samples or checked postconditions, and distinguish no work arriving from work silently failing.

sections.title: On-call, incident response, rollback, kill switches, fallback and recovery drills
body: Prepare rollback, kill switches, manual fallback and recovery drills before increasing autonomy. Name the on-call owner and escalation path. A kill switch should stop new side effects and handle in-flight work explicitly. Test the procedure during a controlled exercise; a runbook nobody can execute is weak protection.

sections.title: Production checks and user feedback can reveal failures offline benchmarks miss
body: Treat user reports as evidence to investigate, even when offline evaluations pass. Anthropic's infrastructure postmortem described quality degradation that required production investigation. The practical lesson is to retain representative quality checks and version context; it does not establish that every complaint has the same cause.

sections.title: Root causes into regression cases; reviewed updates rather than uncontrolled self-modification
body: Convert confirmed incidents into reviewed regression cases, then test the targeted fix and related invariants. Improve prompts, tools or policy through a versioned release process. Do not let production feedback automatically rewrite permissions or deploy code. Keep an audit of what changed and why.

sections.title: Realized ROI, adoption, revisit architecture, retire unsuccessful automation
body: Revisit whether users adopt the workflow and whether realized value exceeds maintenance, review and failure costs. Compare with the original baseline and changed process needs. Retire or simplify automation that no longer pays for itself. Continuing because substantial effort was already spent is not an outcome metric.

sections.title: Backup and restore, disaster recovery scope, dependency changes and deprecation
body: Define what backups cover, recovery time and acceptable data loss, then restore into a test environment. Reconcile business actions after restoration. Track dependency deprecation and renewal responsibilities. For this static playbook, Git recovers published content; personal browser notes require the user's exports.

tradeoffs: Shadow execution: observes behavior without business writes; costs include no full action-path evidence. Still needs data controls.
Limited pilot: real feedback at bounded scope; costs include review and monitoring effort. May not cover all traffic.
Staged rollout: limits initial exposure; costs include parallel version operations. Requires meaningful stop signals.

examples.title: Hypothetical worked example
examples.body: A hypothetical prompt update passes offline tests but increases unresolved cases in production. Pause expansion, retain the old version and compare traces by configuration and task segment. Roll back if stop conditions are met, then turn the confirmed failure into a regression case.

examples.title: A release and rollback record
examples.body: Hypothetical release r17: code commit, prompt hash, model identifier, tool schema v4, index v8, memory policy v2 and eval dataset v3. Eligible traffic: internal draft-only requests, maximum 50/day. Owner: named on-call person. Stop conditions: any unauthorized write, unresolved severe privacy event, or sustained review queue above staffed capacity. Rollback artifact: r16 image and compatible state policy. Drill: stop intake, drain/reconcile in-flight operations, switch version, verify a read-only case and inspect pending jobs. Record actual observations and who accepted remaining gaps.

failureModes.symptom: A model or prompt release causes a regression
failureModes.cause: A behavior or configuration change escaped representative checks
failureModes.diagnostic: Compare outcomes by release version and affected segment
failureModes.mitigation: Apply the documented stop condition, roll back and retain evidence

verification: Record evidence for: Are old jobs compatible?
Record evidence for: Can actions be stopped?
Record evidence for: Who receives quality alerts?
Record evidence for: Can recovery be demonstrated?
Exercise the failure case: a model or prompt release causes a regression. Preserve the observed outcome and unresolved limitations.
reconsiderWhen: Version changes, quality reports or realized value drift

title: Lead with decisions, evidence and ownership
summary: Use clear questions and small experiments to guide adoption and engineering practice.

applicability.required: People must decide, approve, adopt, review or own an automation.
applicability.optional: Use a short evidence review for a small reversible experiment; deepen it as consequences and uncertainty grow.
applicability.unnecessary: Do not implement every pattern here. Omit mechanisms that do not address an identified requirement, and record the rationale.

sections.title: Discovery questions, design reviews, proposing options, communicating uncertainty
body: Begin discovery with the current problem, affected users, process owner and evidence of pain. In a design review ask what must be true, what remains unknown and how the proposed action can fail. Offer credible alternatives and a next experiment rather than forcing premature certainty.

sections.title: Executive framing: outcome, evidence, cost, risks, alternatives and next decision
body: Explain proposals to leaders through outcome, evidence, full cost, risk, alternatives and the decision needed now. Separate a demo result from a production claim. A concise recommendation can say 'approve a two-week read-only pilot' without implying approval for autonomous writes.

sections.title: Decision records, assumptions, evidence and revisit triggers
body: Keep decision records short enough to revisit: decision, context, options, evidence, assumptions, owner and trigger. Link to actual artifacts rather than relying on meeting memory. When an assumption changes, reopen the decision instead of treating the old approval as timeless.

sections.title: Adoption, user training, approval UX, review fatigue and capacity
body: Plan adoption with the people who will use and review the system. Measure review time, override rate and missed escalations. A long queue of low-value approvals creates fatigue and can weaken control. Train users on limitations and correction paths, then observe real work rather than counting logins.

sections.title: Clear action/evidence/consequence presentation, manual takeover and corrections
body: Show the proposed action, supporting evidence and likely consequence together. Let a reviewer correct details or take over manually without losing context. Make approval and rejection equally clear. If the person cannot inspect the relevant evidence in the available time, the oversight design is incomplete.

sections.title: Team ownership, handover, documentation, learning-gap assessment
body: Assign ownership for content, code, integrations, evaluation, cost and incidents. Handover includes known gaps, operation commands and recovery evidence. Identify learning gaps through tasks the team must actually perform, such as tracing a failed tool call or designing a representative evaluation.

sections.title: General first-day/week/month guidance for joining an automation team
body: In the first day, map the process and owners; in the first week, reproduce one workflow and its tests; in the first month, ship a small measured improvement with an operating contract. Adapt this sequence to the role. Avoid prescribing an employer's internal architecture without evidence.

sections.title: Transfer backend skills while learning probabilistic-system evaluation
body: Reuse backend strengths: contracts, state machines, concurrency control, observability and failure testing. Add skills for probabilistic output: representative datasets, rubric design, repeated trials and evidence grounding. Models change which failures occur; they do not remove the need for ordinary software engineering.

sections.title: Reusable question-to-guide navigation and daily stage checklists
body: Use stage checklists as questions that lead to evidence and a next action. Start a daily review with unresolved high-consequence items, recent changes and approaching revisit triggers. Link unfamiliar terms to guides. A checklist marked complete without evidence hides uncertainty rather than resolving it.

sections.title: No employer-specific internal assumptions
body: Use hypothetical examples and public sources when sharing this playbook. Do not add private emails, employer details, internal identifiers or credentials to published content. Personal notes remain on this browser, but exports should still be handled carefully if they contain project information.

alternatives.name: Broad platform program
alternatives.limitations: Premature before shared needs are proven

tradeoffs: Small evidence-led pilot: learning with bounded exposure; costs include may delay broad rollout. Needs explicit success criteria.
Manual process improvement: addresses root workflow friction; costs include less visible novelty. May not solve semantic tasks.
Broad platform program: can serve repeated common needs; costs include coordination and investment. Premature before shared needs are proven.
decisionCriteria: Can users correct and take over?

examples.title: Hypothetical worked example
examples.body: A hypothetical new team member spends the first week reproducing one failed workflow and speaking with its reviewers. The first proposal reduces missing evidence in escalations rather than adding another agent. The result is assessed through resolution time and reviewer feedback.

failureModes.cause: Review demand exceeds capacity or evidence is hard to inspect
failureModes.diagnostic: Measure queue age, review time, overrides and missed escalations
failureModes.mitigation: Reduce action scope and redesign the review handoff with users

verification: Record evidence for: What decision is needed now?
Record evidence for: Who owns its consequences?
Record evidence for: What would change our recommendation?
Record evidence for: Can users correct and take over?
Exercise the failure case: approvals become a rubber stamp. Preserve the observed outcome and unresolved limitations.
reconsiderWhen: Ownership, adoption or project assumptions change

title: How an agent harness fits together
summary: Trace the runtime from model output to policy checks, tool effects, durable state and verified completion.

applicability.required: You are building or configuring a runtime that lets a model use tools over multiple steps.
applicability.optional: Use a short evidence review for a small reversible experiment; deepen it as consequences and uncertainty grow.
applicability.unnecessary: Do not implement every pattern here. Omit mechanisms that do not address an identified requirement, and record the rationale.

sections.title: Execution loop: model -> proposed tool calls -> validation -> dispatch -> results -> next step or verified completion
body: An agent harness is the application runtime around a model. Its basic loop assembles context, asks the model, validates proposed tool calls, checks policy, dispatches tools, records results and either continues or verifies completion. Every transition needs explicit failure and stop behavior; the model is only one component.

sections.title: Model adapters, structured outputs, streaming and usage accounting
body: Adapters translate provider request and response formats into an application contract. Handle streaming interruption, malformed outputs and partial usage reports. Record actual model/configuration identity and account for calls that fail after dispatch. Validate structured output before handing it to domain logic.

sections.title: Tool registry, selection, schemas, policy checks, dispatch and result normalization
body: The tool registry describes capabilities, but a separate policy check decides whether a particular call is allowed now. Dispatchers normalize success, rejection, transient error and unknown outcome. Keep business identifiers and operation keys intact. Tool availability must not be confused with authority to use it.

sections.title: Context assembly and compaction; instruction/data trust separation
body: Context assembly selects the active goal, constraints, state and needed evidence. Compaction should preserve pending actions and exact IDs in structured artifacts. Keep untrusted data distinct from instructions and refresh authoritative policy outside the model. See the context guide for preservation and isolation tests.

sections.title: State/checkpoint management and restoration
body: Persist enough state to identify the current task, owned operations, approvals, versions and verified milestones. A checkpoint should be recoverable after process loss. Restoring conversation alone may repeat completed effects. See durable execution for replay, fencing and uncertain-outcome reconciliation.

sections.title: Memory/retrieval hooks and isolation
body: Retrieve evidence under the caller's access scope and apply an explicit memory-write policy. Keep execution state separate from recalled preferences. Corrections and deletions must reach derived context. Add hooks only when the task needs them; a stateless classifier does not automatically need long-term memory.

sections.title: Limits, deadlines, retry/cancellation and progress controls
body: Enforce overall deadlines, call/output limits, shared child budgets, retry ownership and cancellation in the runtime. Track actual progress rather than token activity. Budget enough effort for final verification and handoff. The model can propose more work, but the runtime decides whether resources permit it.

sections.title: Authorization, exact-action approvals and sandbox execution
body: Bind approval to exact actions and revalidate before dispatch. Isolate code or browser tools and restrict secrets, filesystem and network access. The harness cannot outsource authorization to a prompt. A tool result containing new instructions remains untrusted evidence, not a policy update.

sections.title: Child agents, handoffs, task ownership, shared budgets and aggregation
body: Give each child a task ID, parent, owner, scoped context, permitted tools and resource allocation. Aggregate results against a contract and preserve disagreements. Propagate cancellation and reject stale results after replanning. Use children for independent work, not as a default wrapper around every function.

sections.title: Verification hooks, traces, evaluation integration and configuration versions
body: Run deterministic postcondition checks where possible and connect evaluation to real outcome evidence. Trace model, tool and policy versions without leaking secrets. A verified completion hook should distinguish accepted, pending, outcome unknown and completed. Reports must not collapse these into a generic success.

sections.title: Worker lifecycle, startup, shutdown, recovery and deployment
body: On startup, recover owned tasks safely; during operation, renew leases and measure progress; on shutdown, stop intake and persist safe state. Handle old workers returning after reassignment. Deployment must preserve checkpoint compatibility or drain old jobs. Use an operating contract and rehearsed recovery procedure.

sections.title: What framework provides versus what application must implement/configure
body: Create a responsibility matrix for the chosen framework: which state, retries, approvals, isolation and metrics it supplies, and which require application code or configuration. Exercise each claimed behavior. A built-in feature with defaults that do not match your workflow is still an implementation task.

sections.title: Thin custom harness versus framework runtime; avoid unnecessary universal frameworks
body: A thin harness can suit a small controlled tool loop and makes behavior visible. A framework can reduce implementation work for complex state and integration, while adding abstractions and upgrade obligations. Choose the smallest option that passes realistic failure tests; avoid building a universal platform before demonstrating need.

sections.title: Teach how components fit together without duplicating entire specialist chapters
body: Follow one hypothetical support request through the loop: retrieve an authorized record, propose a draft, validate recipients, request approval, send with an operation key and verify delivery status. Consult specialist guides for each boundary. This integrated view explains how parts connect without replacing their deeper tests.

tradeoffs: Thin custom harness: transparent small loop; costs include you own control features. Avoid recreating a platform accidentally.
Framework runtime: reusable execution and integrations; costs include conventions and upgrades. Verify defaults and omitted duties.
Durable engine plus model adapter: strong workflow structure; costs include more integration work. Model correctness remains separate.

examples.title: Hypothetical worked example
examples.body: A hypothetical support harness reads a scoped ticket, drafts a reply, validates the recipient, waits for exact-action approval, sends with an operation ID and verifies the send status. The completion message reflects that status. A timeout preserves uncertainty instead of reporting success.

failureModes.cause: Completion relies on model text rather than verified state
failureModes.diagnostic: Compare terminal response with operation records and postconditions
failureModes.mitigation: Keep outcome unknown or pending and require a verification hook

verification: Record evidence for: What does the framework supply?
Record evidence for: Where is policy enforced?
Record evidence for: How is state restored?
Record evidence for: Which check proves completion?
Exercise the failure case: the harness announces completion prematurely. Preserve the observed outcome and unresolved limitations.
reconsiderWhen: New tools, recovery needs or delegation complexity
